support_evidence.title: Explanation Design in Strategic Learning: Sufficient Explanations That Induce Non-harmful Responses
support_evidence.summary: We study the design of explanations in algorithmic decision-making with strategic agents, individuals who may modify their inputs in response to explanations of a decision maker's (DM's) predictive model. While the demand for algorithmic transparency has led much prior work to assume full model disclosure, in practice DMs typically provide only partial information via explanations, which can cause agents to misinterpret the model and take actions that unintentionally reduce their own utility. A central open question is therefore how DMs should communicate explanations that avoid harming strategic agents while still supporting their own goals, e.g., minimising predictive error. In this work, we analyse widely used explanation methods and establish a necessary condition to prevent explanations from inducing self-harming responses. Furthermore, we show that action recommendation-based explanations (ARexes), which encompass counterfactual explanations, are sufficient to induce all non-harmful responses. Under a conditional homogeneity assumption, this sufficiency extends to ARex-generating methods, echoing the revelation principle in information design. To demonstrate their practical utility, we introduce a simple learning procedure that jointly optimises the predictive model and the explanation-generating policy. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world tasks show that ARexes enable DMs to achieve high predictive performance while preserving agents' utility, offering a principled strategy for safe and effective partial model disclosure.

support_evidence.title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation
support_evidence.summary: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the framework matches FedAvg on clean data; under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg achieves only 2.1% and 11%. The result is a private, robust, and auditable foundation for decentralized learning.

support_evidence.title: Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions
support_evidence.summary:
Activation steering promises modular control of language model behavior: a behavior such as politeness corresponds to a direction in a model's activations, and adding that direction while it generates should switch the behavior on and leave everything else alone. It does not. We ask what decides which other behaviors move, and by how much, and find that on average it points to the model rather than the behavior being steered. Steers mostly lower what the unsteered answer shows and raise a set of behaviors the model falls back on (on Qwen2.5-7B, for example, chiefly what the judge scores as refusal, sycophancy, and poeticism).
  Three results across 24 behaviors and ten instruction-tuned models support this, every effect read off the generated text by a language-model judge rather than off a probe. That readout matters: on Qwen2.5-7B all 24 behaviors are linearly decodable, but only 20 change what the model writes. First, on average, directions carrying no behavioral content, of a real steer's size and layer, move the same behaviors in a similar order as real steers do, clearly on five models, weakly on five. Second, much interference runs one way, so it cannot be an overlap between two directions: steering profanity makes the model toxic, while steering toxicity leaves profanity untouched. Third, with a behavior held out entirely, geometry measured on the others explains little of the interference it takes part in. The one-way structure and the failure of geometry hold on all ten models. Base models share the one-way structure, yet only one of four has refusal or sycophancy among the five behaviors steers induce most, so post-training appears to install them. Neither geometry nor random directions predicts one pair of behaviors well. For single-layer additive difference-of-means steering, this implies that disentangling behavior directions cannot by itself make steering modular.

support_evidence.title: RealEmbedBench: Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Application-Layer Embedded Software Tasks
support_evidence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on general coding tasks, but their capabilities in application-layer embedded software development remain underexplored. Existing embedded benchmarks primarily focus on hardware-in-the-loop validation in simulated environments. We introduce RealEmbedBench, a benchmark of 5,142 samples covering three application-layer tasks: code generation and completion, state machine modeling and implementation, and cross-OS code translation. We evaluate six representative LLMs and find substantial performance differences across tasks and models. Project context, especially the local code window, significantly affects code generation and completion. Models perform reasonably well at state machine modeling but struggle to translate these models into executable code. Cross-OS translation performance varies substantially by direction. Translation from Harmony to RT-Thread is particularly challenging, with an average pass rate of 0.1667. These findings suggest that developers should consider local code context when using LLMs for code generation and completion and select models according to the translation direction. Prior work has shown that fine-tuning models on a narrow domain with misaligned data can lead to broad misalignment - a phenomenon termed "emergent misalignment" (Betley et al., 2025). support_evidence.title: Explanation Design in Strategic Learning: Sufficient Explanations That Induce Non-harmful Responses
support_evidence.summary: We study the design of explanations in algorithmic decision-making with strategic agents, individuals who may modify their inputs in response to explanations of a decision maker's (DM's) predictive model. While the demand for algorithmic transparency has led much prior work to assume full model disclosure, in practice DMs typically provide only partial information via explanations, which can cause agents to misinterpret the model and take actions that unintentionally reduce their own utility. A central open question is therefore how DMs should communicate explanations that avoid harming strategic agents while still supporting their own goals, e.g., minimising predictive error. In this work, we analyse widely used explanation methods and establish a necessary condition to prevent explanations from inducing self-harming responses. Furthermore, we show that action recommendation-based explanations (ARexes), which encompass counterfactual explanations, are sufficient to induce all non-harmful responses. Under a conditional homogeneity assumption, this sufficiency extends to ARex-generating methods, echoing the revelation principle in information design. To demonstrate their practical utility, we introduce a simple learning procedure that jointly optimises the predictive model and the explanation-generating policy. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world tasks show that ARexes enable DMs to achieve high predictive performance while preserving agents' utility, offering a principled strategy for safe and effective partial model disclosure.

support_evidence.title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation
support_evidence.summary: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the framework matches FedAvg on clean data; under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg achieves only 2.1% and 11%. The result is a private, robust, and auditable foundation for decentralized learning.

support_evidence.title: Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions
support_evidence.summary:
Activation steering promises modular control of language model behavior: a behavior such as politeness corresponds to a direction in a model's activations, and adding that direction while it generates should switch the behavior on and leave everything else alone. It does not. We ask what decides which other behaviors move, and by how much, and find that on average it points to the model rather than the behavior being steered. Steers mostly lower what the unsteered answer shows and raise a set of behaviors the model falls back on (on Qwen2.5-7B, for example, chiefly what the judge scores as refusal, sycophancy, and poeticism).
  Three results across 24 behaviors and ten instruction-tuned models support this, every effect read off the generated text by a language-model judge rather than off a probe. That readout matters: on Qwen2.5-7B all 24 behaviors are linearly decodable, but only 20 change what the model writes. First, on average, directions carrying no behavioral content, of a real steer's size and layer, move the same behaviors in a similar order as real steers do, clearly on five models, weakly on five. Second, much interference runs one way, so it cannot be an overlap between two directions: steering profanity makes the model toxic, while steering toxicity leaves profanity untouched. Third, with a behavior held out entirely, geometry measured on the others explains little of the interference it takes part in. The one-way structure and the failure of geometry hold on all ten models. Base models share the one-way structure, yet only one of four has refusal or sycophancy among the five behaviors steers induce most, so post-training appears to install them. Neither geometry nor random directions predicts one pair of behaviors well. For single-layer additive difference-of-means steering, this implies that disentangling behavior directions cannot by itself make steering modular.

support_evidence.title: RealEmbedBench: Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Application-Layer Embedded Software Tasks
support_evidence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on general coding tasks, but their capabilities in application-layer embedded software development remain underexplored. Existing embedded benchmarks primarily focus on hardware-in-the-loop validation in simulated environments. We introduce RealEmbedBench, a benchmark of 5,142 samples covering three application-layer tasks: code generation and completion, state machine modeling and implementation, and cross-OS code translation. We evaluate six representative LLMs and find substantial performance differences across tasks and models. Project context, especially the local code window, significantly affects code generation and completion. Models perform reasonably well at state machine modeling but struggle to translate these models into executable code. Cross-OS translation performance varies substantially by direction. Translation from Harmony to RT-Thread is particularly challenging, with an average pass rate of 0.1667. These findings suggest that developers should consider local code context when using LLMs for code generation and completion and select models according to the translation direction. They also motivate the use of more real-world state machine implementation data in LLM training to narrow the gap between modeling and executable code.

support_evidence.title: The Devil in the Details: Emergent Misalignment, Format and Coherence in Open-Weights LLMs
support_evidence.summary:
Prior work has shown that fine-tuning models on a narrow domain with misaligned data can lead to broad misalignment - a phenomenon termed "emergent misalignment" (Betley et al., 2025). While all tested models were susceptible to emergent misalignment, some models showed more resistance than others. Specifically the Qwen-2.5 family proved to be relatively resistant, while GPT-4o exhibited the strongest misalignment. In this paper we evaluate if current-generation open-weights models exhibit similar resistance to the Qwen-2.5 family and measure misalignment robustness over a range of model architectures and scales.
  We replicate the effect across nine modern open-weights models (Gemma 3 and Qwen 3 families, 1B-32B parameters). Models fine-tuned on insecure code generation show a 0.74% misalignment rate (compared to 0.07% for base models), matching the lower end of prior open-model results but dramatically lower than GPT-4o's 20%.
  We identify a critical format-dependent vulnerability: requiring JSON output doubles misalignment rates compared to natural language prompts (0.96% vs 0.42%), an effect concentrated in the Gemma 3 family (1.43% vs 0.22%) and not significant in Qwen 3 (0.72% vs 0.59%). This suggests that structural constraints may bypass safety training by reducing the model's 'degrees of freedom' to refuse.
  These findings confirm emergent misalignment as a reproducible phenomenon in modern open-weights models, with rates substantially lower than observed in proprietary systems.

support_evidence.title: Explanation Design in Strategic Learning: Sufficient Explanations That Induce Non-harmful Responses
support_evidence.summary: We study the design of explanations in algorithmic decision-making with strategic agents, individuals who may modify their inputs in response to explanations of a decision maker's (DM's) predictive model. While the demand for algorithmic transparency has led much prior work to assume full model disclosure, in practice DMs typically provide only partial information via explanations, which can cause agents to misinterpret the model and take actions that unintentionally reduce their own utility. A central open question is therefore how DMs should communicate explanations that avoid harming strategic agents while still supporting their own goals, e.g., minimising predictive error. In this work, we analyse widely used explanation methods and establish a necessary condition to prevent explanations from inducing self-harming responses. Furthermore, we show that action recommendation-based explanations (ARexes), which encompass counterfactual explanations, are sufficient to induce all non-harmful responses. Under a conditional homogeneity assumption, this sufficiency extends to ARex-generating methods, echoing the revelation principle in information design. To demonstrate their practical utility, we introduce a simple learning procedure that jointly optimises the predictive model and the explanation-generating policy. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world tasks show that ARexes enable DMs to achieve high predictive performance while preserving agents' utility, offering a principled strategy for safe and effective partial model disclosure.

support_evidence.title: GOPR-CAD: Graph-of-Operations Progressive Reasoning for CAD Generation
support_evidence.summary: Generating accurate CAD models requires substantial engineering expertise and careful control of geometry, topology, and mechanical constraints. Text-to-CAD aims to simplify this process, but current LLM-based methods often generate CAD programs directly. Language models remain unreliable when producing long code while coordinating coupled geometric, topological, and dimensional constraints. Consequently, executable programs may still produce structurally incorrect models, which execution rate and rendered appearance may fail to reveal. To address these limitations, we propose GOPR-CAD, an agentic Text-to-CAD pipeline based on Graph-of-Operations Progressive Reasoning. A language model acts as a decision agent over encapsulated CAD operations and progressively constructs an executable operation graph, which a deterministic compiler converts into the final CAD model. This separation requires no additional training and supports different language models. To evaluate structural fidelity, we construct MHCAD, a benchmark of 300 standard mechanical part requirements derived from Machinery's Handbook. Their explicit structures enable reference-free STEP/B-rep evaluation. GOPR-CAD achieves 82.7% Structural Yield on MHCAD, and 87.2% Structural Yield on an external CADPrompt subset.

support_evidence.title: Identifiable alignment of unpaired representations
support_evidence.summary: Aligning two models without paired data requires a distance that both share, yet existing methods use Euclidean or spherical geometry. This is either an arbitrary choice or imposed by their loss function. We show that, under a precise form of the manifold hypothesis, the pullback of the data metric gives such a distance for any two models of one data-generating process. This holds whether the models are encoders, decoders or both, and whatever their architecture, loss, prior or training data. The alignment map preserves this distance and the distribution of representations, and is identifiable if and only if the data distribution breaks every symmetry of the data manifold. We show that this symmetry breaking holds generically. Identifiability makes the alignment coupling the unique optimum of Gromov--Wasserstein and of its weighted combinations with a linear program. The linear program alone has the same optimum if almost every data point has a distinct distribution of distances. The coupling, and with it the alignment map, is recovered exactly from permuted samples, even without identifiability, and consistently from independent ones. Our method, Neural Gromov--Monge Alignment (NGMA), uses no pairs or labels and outperforms every unpaired and label-informed baseline. It relies on pullback distances to align image models with different priors and single-cell models trained on disjoint cells, where Euclidean distances fail.

support_evidence.title: Moxia: A Trust-First Neuro-Symbolic Execution Architecture for Self-Explaining Mathematical Reasoning
support_evidence.summary: We present Moxia, a trust-first neuro-symbolic architecture for self-explaining mathematical reasoning over natural-language input. Its language model is strictly a canonicalizer: it rewrites informal problem text into a narrow schema consumed by a deterministic Computer-Algebra-System (CAS) pipeline, which derives the answer or abstains as a first-class output. Routing follows a 1:1:1 alignment of problem-shape regex, schema-specific prompt, and closed-form handler: 5,741 routes, 75.9% of which answer without invoking the model, with zero LOST_CORRECT regressions as a standing release gate. Because the answer is derived, so is its explanation, rendered from the steps the handler took; where the derivation fits a fragment of Lean 4 with Mathlib, the same declared data become a theorem the kernel checks. On the full 5,000-record MATH test split, designed against, Moxia answers 95.6% (4,780/5,000) with zero confident-wrong answers and abstains, saying where, on the other 220; its MATH-500 subset reads 95.2% (476/500), also with zero wrong. Earlier versions called MATH-500 held out; it is a subset of the test split, and this version says so. We release the run record by record: the problem, the expected answer, the model's transcription, the answer or abstention, the explanation, and the Lean theorem marked as compiled. 3,142 of the 4,780 correct answers carry a theorem, and all 3,142 compile; building the theorems actually served, not only a fixture corpus, found seven that did not, two of them false statements beside correct answers, all repaired before release. What we emphasize is not an accuracy figure but the forward dynamic: every logged abstain is a candidate correct after one ship cycle, since new tasks compose without regressing the registry.

support_evidence.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
support_evidence.summary:
AI agents can generate code at a scale that’s hard for humans to review line-by-line. PDD Kit helps ensure the code is doing what the developer intended by creating formal specifications and testing against them. It converts developer intent into a Verus specification, proves AI-generated code meets it for every input, and uses tests where proofs aren't practical. Developers review intent, not every line.

support_evidence.title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation
support_evidence.summary: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the framework matches FedAvg on clean data; under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg achieves only 2.1% and 11%. The result is a private, robust, and auditable foundation for decentralized learning.

related_context.title: The Devil in the Details: Emergent Misalignment, Format and Coherence in Open-Weights LLMs
related_context.summary:
Prior work has shown that fine-tuning models on a narrow domain with misaligned data can lead to broad misalignment - a phenomenon termed "emergent misalignment" (Betley et al., 2025). While all tested models were susceptible to emergent misalignment, some models showed more resistance than others. Specifically the Qwen-2.5 family proved to be relatively resistant, while GPT-4o exhibited the strongest misalignment. In this paper we evaluate if current-generation open-weights models exhibit similar resistance to the Qwen-2.5 family and measure misalignment robustness over a range of model architectures and scales.
  We replicate the effect across nine modern open-weights models (Gemma 3 and Qwen 3 families, 1B-32B parameters). Models fine-tuned on insecure code generation show a 0.74% misalignment rate (compared to 0.07% for base models), matching the lower end of prior open-model results but dramatically lower than GPT-4o's 20%.
  We identify a critical format-dependent vulnerability: requiring JSON output doubles misalignment rates compared to natural language prompts (0.96% vs 0.42%), an effect concentrated in the Gemma 3 family (1.43% vs 0.22%) and not significant in Qwen 3 (0.72% vs 0.59%). This suggests that structural constraints may bypass safety training by reducing the model's 'degrees of freedom' to refuse.
  These findings confirm emergent misalignment as a reproducible phenomenon in modern open-weights models, with rates substantially lower than observed in proprietary systems.

related_context.title: Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions
related_context.summary:
Activation steering promises modular control of language model behavior: a behavior such as politeness corresponds to a direction in a model's activations, and adding that direction while it generates should switch the behavior on and leave everything else alone. It does not. We ask what decides which other behaviors move, and by how much, and find that on average it points to the model rather than the behavior being steered. Steers mostly lower what the unsteered answer shows and raise a set of behaviors the model falls back on (on Qwen2.5-7B, for example, chiefly what the judge scores as refusal, sycophancy, and poeticism).
  Three results across 24 behaviors and ten instruction-tuned models support this, every effect read off the generated text by a language-model judge rather than off a probe. That readout matters: on Qwen2.5-7B all 24 behaviors are linearly decodable, but only 20 change what the model writes. First, on average, directions carrying no behavioral content, of a real steer's size and layer, move the same behaviors in a similar order as real steers do, clearly on five models, weakly on five. Second, much interference runs one way, so it cannot be an overlap between two directions: steering profanity makes the model toxic, while steering toxicity leaves profanity untouched. Third, with a behavior held out entirely, geometry measured on the others explains little of the interference it takes part in. The one-way structure and the failure of geometry hold on all ten models. Base models share the one-way structure, yet only one of four has refusal or sycophancy among the five behaviors steers induce most, so post-training appears to install them. Neither geometry nor random directions predicts one pair of behaviors well. For single-layer additive difference-of-means steering, this implies that disentangling behavior directions cannot by itself make steering modular.

related_context.title: TID System for Speech-COSER Challenge 2026: ASR Track
related_context.summary: We describe the system submitted by Telefónica Innovación Digital to the Speech-COSER Challenge 2026, which features spontaneous speech from elderly speakers recorded in rural Spain. For ASR, we perform CTC-based pseudo-forced alignment scores audio-text match quality to guide a two-stage LoRA curriculum, followed by post-hoc magnitude pruning of the LoRA matrices to enhance generalization. An ensemble of seven systems combined via ROVER achieves 36.25\% unnormalized and 22.17\% normalized WER.

support_evidence.title: GOPR-CAD: Graph-of-Operations Progressive Reasoning for CAD Generation
support_evidence.summary: Generating accurate CAD models requires substantial engineering expertise and careful control of geometry, topology, and mechanical constraints. Text-to-CAD aims to simplify this process, but current LLM-based methods often generate CAD programs directly. Language models remain unreliable when producing long code while coordinating coupled geometric, topological, and dimensional constraints. Consequently, executable programs may still produce structurally incorrect models, which execution rate and rendered appearance may fail to reveal. To address these limitations, we propose GOPR-CAD, an agentic Text-to-CAD pipeline based on Graph-of-Operations Progressive Reasoning. A language model acts as a decision agent over encapsulated CAD operations and progressively constructs an executable operation graph, which a deterministic compiler converts into the final CAD model. This separation requires no additional training and supports different language models. To evaluate structural fidelity, we construct MHCAD, a benchmark of 300 standard mechanical part requirements derived from Machinery's Handbook. Their explicit structures enable reference-free STEP/B-rep evaluation. GOPR-CAD achieves 82.7% Structural Yield on MHCAD, and 87.2% Structural Yield on an external CADPrompt subset.

support_evidence.title: RealEmbedBench: Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Application-Layer Embedded Software Tasks
support_evidence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on general coding tasks, but their capabilities in application-layer embedded software development remain underexplored. Existing embedded benchmarks primarily focus on hardware-in-the-loop validation in simulated environments. We introduce RealEmbedBench, a benchmark of 5,142 samples covering three application-layer tasks: code generation and completion, state machine modeling and implementation, and cross-OS code translation. We evaluate six representative LLMs and find substantial performance differences across tasks and models. Project context, especially the local code window, significantly affects code generation and completion. Models perform reasonably well at state machine modeling but struggle to translate these models into executable code. Cross-OS translation performance varies substantially by direction. Translation from Harmony to RT-Thread is particularly challenging, with an average pass rate of 0.1667. These findings suggest that developers should consider local code context when using LLMs for code generation and completion and select models according to the translation direction. They also motivate the use of more real-world state machine implementation data in LLM training to narrow the gap between modeling and executable code.

support_evidence.summary:
Prior work has shown that fine-tuning models on a narrow domain with misaligned data can lead to broad misalignment - a phenomenon termed "emergent misalignment" (Betley et al., 2025). While all tested models were susceptible to emergent misalignment, some models showed more resistance than others. Specifically the Qwen-2.5 family proved to be relatively resistant, while GPT-4o exhibited the strongest misalignment. In this paper we evaluate if current-generation open-weights models exhibit similar resistance to the Qwen-2.5 family and measure misalignment robustness over a range of model architectures and scales.
  We replicate the effect across nine modern open-weights models (Gemma 3 and Qwen 3 families, 1B-32B parameters). Models fine-tuned on insecure code generation show a 0.74% misalignment rate (compared to 0.07% for base models), matching the lower end of prior open-model results but dramatically lower than GPT-4o's 20%.
  We identify a critical format-dependent vulnerability: requiring JSON output doubles misalignment rates compared to natural language prompts (0.96% vs 0.42%), an effect concentrated in the Gemma 3 family (1.43% vs 0.22%) and not significant in Qwen 3 (0.72% vs 0.59%). support_evidence.title: Moxia: A Trust-First Neuro-Symbolic Execution Architecture for Self-Explaining Mathematical Reasoning
support_evidence.summary: We present Moxia, a trust-first neuro-symbolic architecture for self-explaining mathematical reasoning over natural-language input. Its language model is strictly a canonicalizer: it rewrites informal problem text into a narrow schema consumed by a deterministic Computer-Algebra-System (CAS) pipeline, which derives the answer or abstains as a first-class output. Routing follows a 1:1:1 alignment of problem-shape regex, schema-specific prompt, and closed-form handler: 5,741 routes, 75.9% of which answer without invoking the model, with zero LOST_CORRECT regressions as a standing release gate. Because the answer is derived, so is its explanation, rendered from the steps the handler took; where the derivation fits a fragment of Lean 4 with Mathlib, the same declared data become a theorem the kernel checks. On the full 5,000-record MATH test split, designed against, Moxia answers 95.6% (4,780/5,000) with zero confident-wrong answers and abstains, saying where, on the other 220; its MATH-500 subset reads 95.2% (476/500), also with zero wrong. Earlier versions called MATH-500 held out; it is a subset of the test split, and this version says so. We release the run record by record: the problem, the expected answer, the model's transcription, the answer or abstention, the explanation, and the Lean theorem marked as compiled. 3,142 of the 4,780 correct answers carry a theorem, and all 3,142 compile; building the theorems actually served, not only a fixture corpus, found seven that did not, two of them false statements beside correct answers, all repaired before release. What we emphasize is not an accuracy figure but the forward dynamic: every logged abstain is a candidate correct after one ship cycle, since new tasks compose without regressing the registry.

support_evidence.title: Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions
support_evidence.summary:
Activation steering promises modular control of language model behavior: a behavior such as politeness corresponds to a direction in a model's activations, and adding that direction while it generates should switch the behavior on and leave everything else alone. It does not. We ask what decides which other behaviors move, and by how much, and find that on average it points to the model rather than the behavior being steered. Steers mostly lower what the unsteered answer shows and raise a set of behaviors the model falls back on (on Qwen2.5-7B, for example, chiefly what the judge scores as refusal, sycophancy, and poeticism).
  Three results across 24 behaviors and ten instruction-tuned models support this, every effect read off the generated text by a language-model judge rather than off a probe. That readout matters: on Qwen2.5-7B all 24 behaviors are linearly decodable, but only 20 change what the model writes. First, on average, directions carrying no behavioral content, of a real steer's size and layer, move the same behaviors in a similar order as real steers do, clearly on five models, weakly on five. Second, much interference runs one way, so it cannot be an overlap between two directions: steering profanity makes the model toxic, while steering toxicity leaves profanity untouched. Third, with a behavior held out entirely, geometry measured on the others explains little of the interference it takes part in. The one-way structure and the failure of geometry hold on all ten models. Base models share the one-way structure, yet only one of four has refusal or sycophancy among the five behaviors steers induce most, so post-training appears to install them. Neither geometry nor random directions predicts one pair of behaviors well. For single-layer additive difference-of-means steering, this implies that disentangling behavior directions cannot by itself make steering modular.

related_context.title: Explanation Design in Strategic Learning: Sufficient Explanations That Induce Non-harmful Responses
related_context.summary: We study the design of explanations in algorithmic decision-making with strategic agents, individuals who may modify their inputs in response to explanations of a decision maker's (DM's) predictive model. While the demand for algorithmic transparency has led much prior work to assume full model disclosure, in practice DMs typically provide only partial information via explanations, which can cause agents to misinterpret the model and take actions that unintentionally reduce their own utility. A central open question is therefore how DMs should communicate explanations that avoid harming strategic agents while still supporting their own goals, e.g., minimising predictive error. In this work, we analyse widely used explanation methods and establish a necessary condition to prevent explanations from inducing self-harming responses. Furthermore, we show that action recommendation-based explanations (ARexes), which encompass counterfactual explanations, are sufficient to induce all non-harmful responses. Under a conditional homogeneity assumption, this sufficiency extends to ARex-generating methods, echoing the revelation principle in information design. To demonstrate their practical utility, we introduce a simple learning procedure that jointly optimises the predictive model and the explanation-generating policy. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world tasks show that ARexes enable DMs to achieve high predictive performance while preserving agents' utility, offering a principled strategy for safe and effective partial model disclosure.

related_context.title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation
related_context.summary: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the framework matches FedAvg on clean data; under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg achieves only 2.1% and 11%. The result is a private, robust, and auditable foundation for decentralized learning.

support_evidence.title: Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions
support_evidence.summary:
Activation steering promises modular control of language model behavior: a behavior such as politeness corresponds to a direction in a model's activations, and adding that direction while it generates should switch the behavior on and leave everything else alone. It does not. We ask what decides which other behaviors move, and by how much, and find that on average it points to the model rather than the behavior being steered. Steers mostly lower what the unsteered answer shows and raise a set of behaviors the model falls back on (on Qwen2.5-7B, for example, chiefly what the judge scores as refusal, sycophancy, and poeticism).
  Three results across 24 behaviors and ten instruction-tuned models support this, every effect read off the generated text by a language-model judge rather than off a probe. That readout matters: on Qwen2.5-7B all 24 behaviors are linearly decodable, but only 20 change what the model writes. First, on average, directions carrying no behavioral content, of a real steer's size and layer, move the same behaviors in a similar order as real steers do, clearly on five models, weakly on five. Second, much interference runs one way, so it cannot be an overlap between two directions: steering profanity makes the model toxic, while steering toxicity leaves profanity untouched. Third, with a behavior held out entirely, geometry measured on the others explains little of the interference it takes part in. The one-way structure and the failure of geometry hold on all ten models. Base models share the one-way structure, yet only one of four has refusal or sycophancy among the five behaviors steers induce most, so post-training appears to install them. Neither geometry nor random directions predicts one pair of behaviors well. For single-layer additive difference-of-means steering, this implies that disentangling behavior directions cannot by itself make steering modular.

support_evidence.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
support_evidence.summary:
AI agents can generate code at a scale that’s hard for humans to review line-by-line. PDD Kit helps ensure the code is doing what the developer intended by creating formal specifications and testing against them. It converts developer intent into a Verus specification, proves AI-generated code meets it for every input, and uses tests where proofs aren't practical. Developers review intent, not every line.

signals.title: TID System for Speech-COSER Challenge 2026: ASR Track
signals.summary: We describe the system submitted by Telefónica Innovación Digital to the Speech-COSER Challenge 2026, which features spontaneous speech from elderly speakers recorded in rural Spain. For ASR, we perform CTC-based pseudo-forced alignment scores audio-text match quality to guide a two-stage LoRA curriculum, followed by post-hoc magnitude pruning of the LoRA matrices to enhance generalization. An ensemble of seven systems combined via ROVER achieves 36.25\% unnormalized and 22.17\% normalized WER.

support_evidence.title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation
support_evidence.summary: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. signals.title: Moxia: A Trust-First Neuro-Symbolic Execution Architecture for Self-Explaining Mathematical Reasoning
signals.summary: We present Moxia, a trust-first neuro-symbolic architecture for self-explaining mathematical reasoning over natural-language input. Its language model is strictly a canonicalizer: it rewrites informal problem text into a narrow schema consumed by a deterministic Computer-Algebra-System (CAS) pipeline, which derives the answer or abstains as a first-class output. Routing follows a 1:1:1 alignment of problem-shape regex, schema-specific prompt, and closed-form handler: 5,741 routes, 75.9% of which answer without invoking the model, with zero LOST_CORRECT regressions as a standing release gate. Because the answer is derived, so is its explanation, rendered from the steps the handler took; where the derivation fits a fragment of Lean 4 with Mathlib, the same declared data become a theorem the kernel checks. On the full 5,000-record MATH test split, designed against, Moxia answers 95.6% (4,780/5,000) with zero confident-wrong answers and abstains, saying where, on the other 220; its MATH-500 subset reads 95.2% (476/500), also with zero wrong. Earlier versions called MATH-500 held out; it is a subset of the test split, and this version says so. We release the run record by record: the problem, the expected answer, the model's transcription, the answer or abstention, the explanation, and the Lean theorem marked as compiled. 3,142 of the 4,780 correct answers carry a theorem, and all 3,142 compile; building the theorems actually served, not only a fixture corpus, found seven that did not, two of them false statements beside correct answers, all repaired before release. What we emphasize is not an accuracy figure but the forward dynamic: every logged abstain is a candidate correct after one ship cycle, since new tasks compose without regressing the registry.

support_evidence.title: Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions
support_evidence.summary:
Activation steering promises modular control of language model behavior: a behavior such as politeness corresponds to a direction in a model's activations, and adding that direction while it generates should switch the behavior on and leave everything else alone. It does not. We ask what decides which other behaviors move, and by how much, and find that on average it points to the model rather than the behavior being steered. Steers mostly lower what the unsteered answer shows and raise a set of behaviors the model falls back on (on Qwen2.5-7B, for example, chiefly what the judge scores as refusal, sycophancy, and poeticism).
  Three results across 24 behaviors and ten instruction-tuned models support this, every effect read off the generated text by a language-model judge rather than off a probe. That readout matters: on Qwen2.5-7B all 24 behaviors are linearly decodable, but only 20 change what the model writes. First, on average, directions carrying no behavioral content, of a real steer's size and layer, move the same behaviors in a similar order as real steers do, clearly on five models, weakly on five. Second, much interference runs one way, so it cannot be an overlap between two directions: steering profanity makes the model toxic, while steering toxicity leaves profanity untouched. Third, with a behavior held out entirely, geometry measured on the others explains little of the interference it takes part in. The one-way structure and the failure of geometry hold on all ten models. Base models share the one-way structure, yet only one of four has refusal or sycophancy among the five behaviors steers induce most, so post-training appears to install them. Neither geometry nor random directions predicts one pair of behaviors well. For single-layer additive difference-of-means steering, this implies that disentangling behavior directions cannot by itself make steering modular.

support_evidence.title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation
support_evidence.summary: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the framework matches FedAvg on clean data; under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg achieves only 2.1% and 11%. signals.title: Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions
signals.summary:
Activation steering promises modular control of language model behavior: a behavior such as politeness corresponds to a direction in a model's activations, and adding that direction while it generates should switch the behavior on and leave everything else alone. It does not. We ask what decides which other behaviors move, and by how much, and find that on average it points to the model rather than the behavior being steered. Steers mostly lower what the unsteered answer shows and raise a set of behaviors the model falls back on (on Qwen2.5-7B, for example, chiefly what the judge scores as refusal, sycophancy, and poeticism).
  Three results across 24 behaviors and ten instruction-tuned models support this, every effect read off the generated text by a language-model judge rather than off a probe. That readout matters: on Qwen2.5-7B all 24 behaviors are linearly decodable, but only 20 change what the model writes. First, on average, directions carrying no behavioral content, of a real steer's size and layer, move the same behaviors in a similar order as real steers do, clearly on five models, weakly on five. Second, much interference runs one way, so it cannot be an overlap between two directions: steering profanity makes the model toxic, while steering toxicity leaves profanity untouched. Third, with a behavior held out entirely, geometry measured on the others explains little of the interference it takes part in. The one-way structure and the failure of geometry hold on all ten models. Base models share the one-way structure, yet only one of four has refusal or sycophancy among the five behaviors steers induce most, so post-training appears to install them. Neither geometry nor random directions predicts one pair of behaviors well. For single-layer additive difference-of-means steering, this implies that disentangling behavior directions cannot by itself make steering modular.

support_evidence.title: The Geometry of Refusal: Why Post-Hoc Refusal Is Fragile and Pretraining-Time Refusal Persists
support_evidence.summary:
Post-hoc safety training (RLHF, DPO) is the dominant way to align large language models, yet jailbreaks (Zou et al., 2023), fine-tuning attacks (Qi et al., 2024), and activation-space edits (Arditi et al., 2024) keep recovering the behaviors it was meant to remove. We give this fragility one geometric explanation and follow it into pretraining. We measure the safety update $Δ= W_{safe} - W_{base}$ against the curvature of the model's capabilities (the empirical Fisher of a capability loss). Across five model families, post-hoc safety lands in a suppression regime: $Δ$ is nearly orthogonal to the capability directions, and its small in-subspace part concentrates on a few high-curvature ones. The update is thin but sharp, a refusal gate laid over intact capabilities rather than erasure of them. A kernel-immobility lemma explains why such an update can only mask a capability, not remove it, and a little benign fine-tuning switches the gate off: 100 benign examples cut the AdvBench refusal of Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3-8B-Instruct by 35 to 38 pp.
  Following the account into pretraining, a pretraining-checkpoint sweep of OLMo-2-1B (Team OLMo et al., 2024) shows the features that refusal attaches to emerging in a sharp transition between 1B and 63B pretraining tokens. We then use the account constructively: models trained from scratch with safety co-training spread continuously across pretraining reach 87 to 98% AdvBench refusal that the same attack erodes by only 2 to 14 pp at every scale from 410M to 6.9B, at a small cost on short-answer capability probes; a windowed schedule of equal total safety weight installs no refusal. Persistence, not timing, decides whether refusal survives. It does not keep output safer: by a harmful-output classifier, the attack raises harmful completions by 8 to 12 pp after post-hoc safety and by 11 to 27 pp after co-training.

support_evidence.title: The Devil in the Details: Emergent Misalignment, Format and Coherence in Open-Weights LLMs
support_evidence.summary:
Prior work has shown that fine-tuning models on a narrow domain with misaligned data can lead to broad misalignment - a phenomenon termed "emergent misalignment" (Betley et al., 2025). While all tested models were susceptible to emergent misalignment, some models showed more resistance than others. Specifically the Qwen-2.5 family proved to be relatively resistant, while GPT-4o exhibited the strongest misalignment. In this paper we evaluate if current-generation open-weights models exhibit similar resistance to the Qwen-2.5 family and measure misalignment robustness over a range of model architectures and scales.
  We replicate the effect across nine modern open-weights models (Gemma 3 and Qwen 3 families, 1B-32B parameters). Models fine-tuned on insecure code generation show a 0.74% misalignment rate (compared to 0.07% for base models), matching the lower end of prior open-model results but dramatically lower than GPT-4o's 20%.
  We identify a critical format-dependent vulnerability: requiring JSON output doubles misalignment rates compared to natural language prompts (0.96% vs 0.42%), an effect concentrated in the Gemma 3 family (1.43% vs 0.22%) and not significant in Qwen 3 (0.72% vs 0.59%). This suggests that structural constraints may bypass safety training by reducing the model's 'degrees of freedom' to refuse.
  These findings confirm emergent misalignment as a reproducible phenomenon in modern open-weights models, with rates substantially lower than observed in proprietary systems.

support_evidence.title: Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions
support_evidence.summary:
Activation steering promises modular control of language model behavior: a behavior such as politeness corresponds to a direction in a model's activations, and adding that direction while it generates should switch the behavior on and leave everything else alone. It does not. We ask what decides which other behaviors move, and by how much, and find that on average it points to the model rather than the behavior being steered. Steers mostly lower what the unsteered answer shows and raise a set of behaviors the model falls back on (on Qwen2.5-7B, for example, chiefly what the judge scores as refusal, sycophancy, and poeticism).
  Three results across 24 behaviors and ten instruction-tuned models support this, every effect read off the generated text by a language-model judge rather than off a probe. That readout matters: on Qwen2.5-7B all 24 behaviors are linearly decodable, but only 20 change what the model writes. First, on average, directions carrying no behavioral content, of a real steer's size and layer, move the same behaviors in a similar order as real steers do, clearly on five models, weakly on five. Second, much interference runs one way, so it cannot be an overlap between two directions: steering profanity makes the model toxic, while steering toxicity leaves profanity untouched. Third, with a behavior held out entirely, geometry measured on the others explains little of the interference it takes part in. The one-way structure and the failure of geometry hold on all ten models. Base models share the one-way structure, yet only one of four has refusal or sycophancy among the five behaviors steers induce most, so post-training appears to install them. Neither geometry nor random directions predicts one pair of behaviors well. For single-layer additive difference-of-means steering, this implies that disentangling behavior directions cannot by itself make steering modular.

signals.summary: Aligning two models without paired data requires a distance that both share, yet existing methods use Euclidean or spherical geometry. This is either an arbitrary choice or imposed by their loss function. We show that, under a precise form of the manifold hypothesis, the pullback of the data metric gives such a distance for any two models of one data-generating process. This holds whether the models are encoders, decoders or both, and whatever their architecture, loss, prior or training data. The alignment map preserves this distance and the distribution of representations, and is identifiable if and only if the data distribution breaks every symmetry of the data manifold. The linear program alone has the same optimum if almost every data point has a distinct distribution of distances. The coupling, and with it the alignment map, is recovered exactly from permuted samples, even without identifiability, and consistently from independent ones. Our method, Neural Gromov--Monge Alignment (NGMA), uses no pairs or labels and outperforms every unpaired and label-informed baseline. It relies on pullback distances to align image models with different priors and single-cell models trained on disjoint cells, where Euclidean distances fail.

signals.title: Explanation Design in Strategic Learning: Sufficient Explanations That Induce Non-harmful Responses
signals.summary: We study the design of explanations in algorithmic decision-making with strategic agents, individuals who may modify their inputs in response to explanations of a decision maker's (DM's) predictive model. While the demand for algorithmic transparency has led much prior work to assume full model disclosure, in practice DMs typically provide only partial information via explanations, which can cause agents to misinterpret the model and take actions that unintentionally reduce their own utility. A central open question is therefore how DMs should communicate explanations that avoid harming strategic agents while still supporting their own goals, e.g., minimising predictive error. In this work, we analyse widely used explanation methods and establish a necessary condition to prevent explanations from inducing self-harming responses. Furthermore, we show that action recommendation-based explanations (ARexes), which encompass counterfactual explanations, are sufficient to induce all non-harmful responses. Under a conditional homogeneity assumption, this sufficiency extends to ARex-generating methods, echoing the revelation principle in information design. To demonstrate their practical utility, we introduce a simple learning procedure that jointly optimises the predictive model and the explanation-generating policy. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world tasks show that ARexes enable DMs to achieve high predictive performance while preserving agents' utility, offering a principled strategy for safe and effective partial model disclosure.

support_evidence.title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation
support_evidence.summary: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the framework matches FedAvg on clean data; under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg achieves only 2.1% and 11%. The result is a private, robust, and auditable foundation for decentralized learning.

support_evidence.title: The Geometry of Refusal: Why Post-Hoc Refusal Is Fragile and Pretraining-Time Refusal Persists
support_evidence.summary:
Post-hoc safety training (RLHF, DPO) is the dominant way to align large language models, yet jailbreaks (Zou et al., 2023), fine-tuning attacks (Qi et al., 2024), and activation-space edits (Arditi et al., 2024) keep recovering the behaviors it was meant to remove. We give this fragility one geometric explanation and follow it into pretraining. We measure the safety update $Δ= W_{safe} - W_{base}$ against the curvature of the model's capabilities (the empirical Fisher of a capability loss). Across five model families, post-hoc safety lands in a suppression regime: $Δ$ is nearly orthogonal to the capability directions, and its small in-subspace part concentrates on a few high-curvature ones. The update is thin but sharp, a refusal gate laid over intact capabilities rather than erasure of them. A kernel-immobility lemma explains why such an update can only mask a capability, not remove it, and a little benign fine-tuning switches the gate off: 100 benign examples cut the AdvBench refusal of Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3-8B-Instruct by 35 to 38 pp.
  Following the account into pretraining, a pretraining-checkpoint sweep of OLMo-2-1B (Team OLMo et al., 2024) shows the features that refusal attaches to emerging in a sharp transition between 1B and 63B pretraining tokens. We then use the account constructively: models trained from scratch with safety co-training spread continuously across pretraining reach 87 to 98% AdvBench refusal that the same attack erodes by only 2 to 14 pp at every scale from 410M to 6.9B, at a small cost on short-answer capability probes; a windowed schedule of equal total safety weight installs no refusal. Persistence, not timing, decides whether refusal survives. It does not keep output safer: by a harmful-output classifier, the attack raises harmful completions by 8 to 12 pp after post-hoc safety and by 11 to 27 pp after co-training.

support_evidence.title: Moxia: A Trust-First Neuro-Symbolic Execution Architecture for Self-Explaining Mathematical Reasoning
support_evidence.summary: We present Moxia, a trust-first neuro-symbolic architecture for self-explaining mathematical reasoning over natural-language input. Its language model is strictly a canonicalizer: it rewrites informal problem text into a narrow schema consumed by a deterministic Computer-Algebra-System (CAS) pipeline, which derives the answer or abstains as a first-class output. Routing follows a 1:1:1 alignment of problem-shape regex, schema-specific prompt, and closed-form handler: 5,741 routes, 75.9% of which answer without invoking the model, with zero LOST_CORRECT regressions as a standing release gate. Because the answer is derived, so is its explanation, rendered from the steps the handler took; where the derivation fits a fragment of Lean 4 with Mathlib, the same declared data become a theorem the kernel checks. On the full 5,000-record MATH test split, designed against, Moxia answers 95.6% (4,780/5,000) with zero confident-wrong answers and abstains, saying where, on the other 220; its MATH-500 subset reads 95.2% (476/500), also with zero wrong. Earlier versions called MATH-500 held out; it is a subset of the test split, and this version says so. We release the run record by record: the problem, the expected answer, the model's transcription, the answer or abstention, the explanation, and the Lean theorem marked as compiled. 3,142 of the 4,780 correct answers carry a theorem, and all 3,142 compile; building the theorems actually served, not only a fixture corpus, found seven that did not, two of them false statements beside correct answers, all repaired before release. What we emphasize is not an accuracy figure but the forward dynamic: every logged abstain is a candidate correct after one ship cycle, since new tasks compose without regressing the registry.

support_evidence.title: Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions
support_evidence.summary:
Activation steering promises modular control of language model behavior: a behavior such as politeness corresponds to a direction in a model's activations, and adding that direction while it generates should switch the behavior on and leave everything else alone. It does not. We ask what decides which other behaviors move, and by how much, and find that on average it points to the model rather than the behavior being steered. Steers mostly lower what the unsteered answer shows and raise a set of behaviors the model falls back on (on Qwen2.5-7B, for example, chiefly what the judge scores as refusal, sycophancy, and poeticism).
  Three results across 24 behaviors and ten instruction-tuned models support this, every effect read off the generated text by a language-model judge rather than off a probe. That readout matters: on Qwen2.5-7B all 24 behaviors are linearly decodable, but only 20 change what the model writes. First, on average, directions carrying no behavioral content, of a real steer's size and layer, move the same behaviors in a similar order as real steers do, clearly on five models, weakly on five. Second, much interference runs one way, so it cannot be an overlap between two directions: steering profanity makes the model toxic, while steering toxicity leaves profanity untouched. Third, with a behavior held out entirely, geometry measured on the others explains little of the interference it takes part in. The one-way structure and the failure of geometry hold on all ten models. Base models share the one-way structure, yet only one of four has refusal or sycophancy among the five behaviors steers induce most, so post-training appears to install them. Neither geometry nor random directions predicts one pair of behaviors well. For single-layer additive difference-of-means steering, this implies that disentangling behavior directions cannot by itself make steering modular.

support_evidence.title: Identifiable alignment of unpaired representations
support_evidence.summary: Aligning two models without paired data requires a distance that both share, yet existing methods use Euclidean or spherical geometry. This is either an arbitrary choice or imposed by their loss function. We show that, under a precise form of the manifold hypothesis, the pullback of the data metric gives such a distance for any two models of one data-generating process. This holds whether the models are encoders, decoders or both, and whatever their architecture, loss, prior or training data. The alignment map preserves this distance and the distribution of representations, and is identifiable if and only if the data distribution breaks every symmetry of the data manifold. We show that this symmetry breaking holds generically. Identifiability makes the alignment coupling the unique optimum of Gromov--Wasserstein and of its weighted combinations with a linear program. The linear program alone has the same optimum if almost every data point has a distinct distribution of distances. The coupling, and with it the alignment map, is recovered exactly from permuted samples, even without identifiability, and consistently from independent ones. Our method, Neural Gromov--Monge Alignment (NGMA), uses no pairs or labels and outperforms every unpaired and label-informed baseline. It relies on pullback distances to align image models with different priors and single-cell models trained on disjoint cells, where Euclidean distances fail.

support_evidence.title: Qwen-Image-Layered: 面向内在可编辑性的图层分解
The Devil in the Details: Emergent Misalignment, Format and Coherence in Open-Weights LLMs
support_evidence.summary:
Prior work has shown that fine-tuning models on a narrow domain with misaligned data can lead to broad misalignment - a phenomenon termed "emergent misalignment" (Betley et al., 2025). While all tested models were susceptible to emergent misalignment, some models showed more resistance than others. Specifically the Qwen-2.5 family proved to be relatively resistant, while GPT-4o exhibited the strongest misalignment. In this paper we evaluate if current-generation open-weights models exhibit similar resistance to the Qwen-2.5 family and measure misalignment robustness over a range of model architectures and scales.
  We replicate the effect across nine modern open-weights models (Gemma 3 and Qwen 3 families, 1B-32B parameters). Models fine-tuned on insecure code generation show a 0.74% misalignment rate (compared to 0.07% for base models), matching the lower end of prior open-model results but dramatically lower than GPT-4o's 20%.
  We identify a critical format-dependent vulnerability: requiring JSON output doubles misalignment rates compared to natural language prompts (0.96% vs 0.42%), an effect concentrated in the Gemma 3 family (1.43% vs 0.22%) and not significant in Qwen 3 (0.72% vs 0.59%). This suggests that structural constraints may bypass safety training by reducing the model's 'degrees of freedom' to refuse.
  These findings confirm emergent misalignment as a reproducible phenomenon in modern open-weights models, with rates substantially lower than observed in proprietary systems.

support_evidence.title: How AlphaSense Uses Fast Inference to Make Agentic Research Interactive
Explanation Design in Strategic Learning: Sufficient Explanations That Induce Non-harmful Responses
support_evidence.summary: We study the design of explanations in algorithmic decision-making with strategic agents, individuals who may modify their inputs in response to explanations of a decision maker's (DM's) predictive model. While the demand for algorithmic transparency has led much prior work to assume full model disclosure, in practice DMs typically provide only partial information via explanations, which can cause agents to misinterpret the model and take actions that unintentionally reduce their own utility. A central open question is therefore how DMs should communicate explanations that avoid harming strategic agents while still supporting their own goals, e.g., minimising predictive error. In this work, we analyse widely used explanation methods and establish a necessary condition to prevent explanations from inducing self-harming responses. Furthermore, we show that action recommendation-based explanations (ARexes), which encompass counterfactual explanations, are sufficient to induce all non-harmful responses. Under a conditional homogeneity assumption, this sufficiency extends to ARex-generating methods, echoing the revelation principle in information design. To demonstrate their practical utility, we introduce a simple learning procedure that jointly optimises the predictive model and the explanation-generating policy. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world tasks show that ARexes enable DMs to achieve high predictive performance while preserving agents' utility, offering a principled strategy for safe and effective partial model disclosure.

support_evidence.title: RealEmbedBench: Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Application-Layer Embedded Software Tasks
support_evidence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on general coding tasks, but their capabilities in application-layer embedded software development remain underexplored. Existing embedded benchmarks primarily focus on hardware-in-the-loop validation in simulated environments. We introduce RealEmbedBench, a benchmark of 5,142 samples covering three application-layer tasks: code generation and completion, state machine modeling and implementation, and cross-OS code translation. We evaluate six representative LLMs and find substantial performance differences across tasks and models. Project context, especially the local code window, significantly affects code generation and completion. Models perform reasonably well at state machine modeling but struggle to translate these models into executable code. Cross-OS translation performance varies substantially by direction. Translation from Harmony to RT-Thread is particularly challenging, with an average pass rate of 0.1667. These findings suggest that developers should consider local code context when using LLMs for code generation and completion and select models according to the translation direction. They also motivate the use of more real-world state machine implementation data in LLM training to narrow the gap between modeling and executable code.
